description: A giant hole spotted above Antarctica, a treaty signed by 197 countries, and a planet that is healing. This is **the only major ecological crisis** humanity has already solved.

hero.hook: A hole in the sky, found by accident, and closed again by a treaty the whole world signed.

blocks.text: In 1985, British scientists stationed in Antarctica could not believe their own measurements: part of the sky seemed to have lost its protection against the Sun. It was not an instrument error but a real hole in the ozone layer, the invisible shield that protects us all. This course tells how the world discovered that danger and how, for once, it managed to repair it.

The **ozone layer** sits between 15 and 35 kilometers up, in the [[Stratosphere]], and it absorbs most of the **UV-B** rays, the part of sunlight strong enough to damage our skin and the DNA of living cells. In the 1930s, industry invented **chlorofluorocarbons**, or [[CFCs]]: gases that looked perfect and cost little, so they went everywhere, into refrigerators, air conditioners and aerosol cans.

The problem is that these gases are too stable. Instead of breaking down near the ground, they rise all the way to the stratosphere. In 1974, the chemists Mario Molina and Frank Sherwood Rowland sounded the alarm: under sunlight, CFCs release chlorine, and chlorine destroys ozone. They would win the Nobel Prize in 1995, but almost nobody listened to them at the time.

sections.title: A fragile shield, a very handy poison

blocks.text: In 1985, the British Antarctic Survey confirmed the news: every spring, a spectacular hole opens in the ozone layer above [[Antarctica]]. NASA satellites already held the same data, but their software had thrown it out as too extreme to be true.

blocks.caption: The ozone hole above Antarctica, seen from space

blocks.text: The threat to human health was taken very seriously, and the world moved fast. In 1987, countries signed [[The Montreal Protocol (1987)]], a treaty that organized the phase-out of CFCs. Only 24 countries signed at first. Today it brings together **197**, every member of the United Nations.
The Montreal Protocol is the only treaty in the history of the United Nations ratified by every country in the world, without exception.

That success came from one clear rule for everyone and a shared fund that helped poorer countries replace their machines. Even manufacturers, hostile at first, fell into line once they found profitable substitutes.

sections.title: 1985: the shock, then the global deal

blocks.text: This success is often cited to argue that climate change could be solved the same way. But the two problems are different. The ozone hole came from a small number of gases made in a small number of factories, which made it easy to target. [[Carbon dioxide (CO₂)]] comes out of almost everything modern society does, from travel and heating to farming and building. Cutting CO₂ means changing the whole world economy, not just a handful of chemical plants.
One bonus along the way: CFCs were also powerful greenhouse gases. By banning them, the Montreal Protocol slowed global warming too, even though that was never its main goal.
Without the treaty, CFCs alone could have added about 1°C of extra warming to the Earth by 2050, purely through their greenhouse effect.
The chlorine already up in the atmosphere takes time to disappear: harmful gas levels only stabilized in the mid-1990s. Since the early 2000s, the recovery has been clear and measurable.

events.title: Back to normal (projected)

blocks.text: If the treaty keeps being respected, the ozone layer should return to its 1980 state around **2065-2070**, preventing millions of skin cancers and cataracts. Vigilance is still needed: illegal CFC emissions were traced to East Asia a few years ago, proof that a global agreement only works when it is monitored without pause.
The ozone hole remains the only major environmental crisis fully solved by global cooperation: a treaty signed in 1987 by 197 countries, with results that scientists can measure.
